The optical 'carpet' cloak is designed using quasi-conformal mapping to conceal an object placed under a curved reflecting surface.
The carpet cloak consists only of isotropic dielectric materials, enabling broadband and low-loss invisibility at a wavelength range of 1,400–1,800 nm.
The carpet cloak was fabricated on a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer, with a 250 nm thick silicon layer serving as the optical slab waveguide.
The cloak region was created by milling a 2D array of holes with varying densities through the silicon layer using focused ion beam (FIB) milling.
The fabricated carpet cloak demonstrated broadband performance from 1,400 to 1,800 nm wavelengths, with a measured transmission of 58% at 1,540 nm.
The cloak was able to transform the curved reflecting surface into a flat, virtual surface, rendering the object underneath invisible.
The all-dielectric carpet cloak design avoids the need for resonant metallic metamaterials, which suffer from high losses and fabrication challenges at optical frequencies.
The quasi-conformal mapping design minimizes the anisotropy of the medium, allowing the use of non-resonant dielectric materials.
The authors suggest that using electron beam lithography and reactive ion etching could further improve the performance and eliminate fabrication-related losses.
This work represents a major step towards realizing practical transformation optics devices at optical frequencies, which has been a long-standing challenge.
The carpet cloak compresses the object in only one direction into a conducting sheet, avoiding the material and geometry singularities associated with other cloaking transformations.

The optical carpet cloaking technology could enable a wide range of applications, such as hiding objects or defects on surfaces, creating illusions or mirage effects, and advancing transformation optics devices.

The cloak was placed around a curved reflecting surface (bump) on the silicon slab waveguide, and a light beam incident on the bump showed a reflection profile identical to that of a beam reflected from a flat surface.
The 2D simulation results showed good agreement with the experimental observations, confirming the cloaking effect.
Measurements were carried out over a wide range of wavelengths from 1,400 to 1,800 nm, demonstrating the broadband performance of the carpet cloak.
